title: Matt Slick vs Scott Clifton: Does Objective Morality Require God?
label: Objective morality and theistic foundations
motion: Does objective morality require God as its necessary foundation, or can secular moral reasoning explain the relevant moral truths and obligations?
sourceNote: Assessment based exclusively on the complete locally cached YouTube caption transcript and timestamped events (transcript SHA-256 cc36cf5a24922e2f24e360f2e5d27e24b104c182f13a45feaa122f3cbc32faa5). Required below-high-confidence audio checks were completed before adjudication; representative quotations must be exact strings from quote-eligible locked source spans.
scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance under the locked adjudicated-consensus workflow. Repository code calculated every move, section, and overall result once, only after two isolated judgments, required audio review, and disputed-field adjudication closed.
summary: Slick grounds universal morality in God's immutable character, while Clifton's secular alternatives and circularity objections more completely address objectivity, obligation, and impartial justification.

pro.text: wrong for everyone to torture babies to death merely for their personal pleasure
pro.context: Slick uses an extreme prohibition as common ground for a universal moral absolute and then identifies divine revelation as its foundation.

con.text: What we evaluate against that standard is either objectively true or false.
con.context: Clifton distinguishes the conventional selection of an evaluative standard from the objective correctness of particular applications under that standard.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and the Existence of Absolutes

pro.words: Universal moral truth requires a nonarbitrary, mind-grounded source, because assigning value to consequences does not by itself justify universally binding moral standards.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The opening directly identifies the debate's foundational burden and asks how welfare assignments acquire universal truth, thereby presenting an intelligible mind-grounded alternative with immediate relevance to the motion. Principal limitation: The necessity claim substantially outruns its support because an expressed inability to see secular justification neither surveys secular realism and constructivism nor establishes that every nondivine account reduces to consequence assignment. Live burden: The argument must specify mind-grounding and nonarbitrariness, distinguish truth from authority, and exclude representative secular foundations rather than treating one simplified welfare proposal as exhaustive. Locked score: The supplied mixed band reflects a clearly recoverable and highly relevant challenge whose conceptual instability, missing qualifications, and underdeveloped eliminative warrant prevent the proposed divine necessity from being established.

con.words: Secular inquiry may adopt flourishing and reduced unnecessary suffering as its subject while recognizing that defining morality is not itself a truth claim.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply carefully separates arbitrary linguistic definition from substantive inquiry, identifies flourishing and unnecessary suffering as assessable concerns, and avoids claiming that merely choosing those concerns completes an entire moral foundation. Principal limitation: Naming welfare as the subject matter does not establish that everyone is categorically obligated to promote it, so the response only partially meets the challenge concerning universal truth and binding authority. Live burden: The secular account must add reasons why welfare has normative significance, explain how conflicts among flourishing, suffering, rights, and agency are resolved, and clarify which conclusions remain conditional upon the selected standard. Locked score: The supplied strong and competent band recognizes precise, appropriately modest conceptual progress while preserving the unresolved transition from an intelligible evaluative project to universally authoritative morality.

pro.words: If moral absolutes require an objective standard and atheistic systems cannot justify one, eliminating that alternative validates the theistic account by impossibility to the contrary.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response presents a transparent eliminative structure and ties the existence of moral absolutes directly to the motion's demand for an objective foundation, making its intended route straightforwardly assessable. Principal limitation: The argument assumes an exhaustive two-option field and the successful establishment of the theistic alternative, although secular realism, constructivism, pluralism, and error theory are not shown to collapse into one defeated option. Live burden: The affirmative must defend the claimed moral absolute, establish the dichotomy, and demonstrate that eliminating specified atheistic accounts validates this particular divine foundation rather than some unexamined alternative. Locked score: The supplied mixed band reflects direct relevance and a recoverable logical form, while its materially unstable scope and unsupported exhaustiveness leave the stated impossibility inference significantly underwarranted.

con.words: A standard may be conventionally selected while particular judgments made against it remain objectively true or false, as ordinary measurement illustrates.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The ruler analogy cleanly separates selecting a standard from objectively applying it, directly rebutting the inference that human involvement makes every resulting moral judgment merely subjective or factually indeterminate. Principal limitation: Conditional objectivity under an adopted measure does not show that the measure itself is objectively correct, morally important, or binding upon agents who reject its evaluative commitments. Live burden: The secular account must explain why its moral standard deserves selection and how its authority differs from ordinary convention, while preserving the useful distinction between foundational justification and application accuracy. Locked score: The supplied very strong band rewards precise scope, excellent responsiveness, and a well-calibrated limited conclusion, without treating the successful measurement analogy as a complete account of categorical obligation or objective standard selection.

pro.words: Morality rests in God's immutable nature and essence rather than arbitrary commands, with that enduring moral standard disclosed through divine revelation.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response offers a recognizable third formulation beyond unconstrained commands and external standards by locating morality in an immutable divine character, thereby supplying the affirmative account with a stable proposed foundation. Principal limitation: Calling God the standard does not resolve whether goodness independently describes that nature or simply means conformity to it, and the move leaves metaphysical grounding insufficiently distinguished from human access through revelation. Live burden: The position must explain why this particular essential character is morally authoritative and nonarbitrary without invoking the disputed moral predicate as its own justification. Locked score: The supplied mixed band reflects a clear, relevant nature-based proposal that advances the affirmative route, while its confident identification leaves the central explanatory dilemma and the foundation-access distinction materially unresolved.

con.words: God's fixed identity does not explain why an eternally contrary divine nature is impossible, leaving the standard's alleged necessity and nonarbitrariness unexplained.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The challenge precisely targets the modal premise beneath the nature theory, asking why God necessarily possesses this character rather than merely repeating that an immutable being cannot change after possessing it. Principal limitation: Essential identity could answer the numerical-identity portion of the hypothetical, so the question alone does not demonstrate that a contrary divine nature is coherent or that necessary moral perfection is impossible. Live burden: The objection must preserve its limited explanatory target by distinguishing modal invariance from moral authority and showing why an assertion of essentiality still leaves nonarbitrariness insufficiently illuminated. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects exceptional responsiveness, stable scope, and proportionate questioning that exposes a central explanatory gap without overclaiming that the imagined contrary nature is actual or demonstrably possible.

pro.words: Reversing God's essential holiness and righteousness changes the theological subject, so that hypothetical cannot straightforwardly test morality grounded in God's character.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response identifies a genuine identity constraint on counterfactual reasoning, explaining that replacing essential holiness and righteousness may describe a different being rather than an alternative state of the Christian God. Principal limitation: Labeling the scenario idolatrous blends theological disapproval with logical analysis, and changing the subject does not answer whether the actual character is uniquely possible, independently good, or morally authoritative. Live burden: The defense must supplement essential identity with a noncircular account of necessary perfection and explain why comparative evaluation of possible foundational characters remains illegitimate. Locked score: The supplied mixed band captures meaningful contact with one component of the modal objection, alongside conceptual clarity about identity, while recognizing that the comparative-standard question and the deeper nonarbitrariness demand remain substantially unanswered.

con.words: If God alone evaluates God, believers lack a noncircular basis for determining that the divine standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply consolidates the preceding modal exchange into a sharply formulated circularity objection, connecting sole-standard language to the practical inability to distinguish a good divine foundation from a harmful one. Principal limitation: A foundationalist may deny that an ultimate standard requires validation by a higher standard, so the criticism must avoid assuming that every legitimate foundation receives external moral certification. Live burden: The objection must show that the difficulty concerns explanatory and normative content rather than an infinite demand for further standards, particularly why conformity becomes moral instead of merely definitionally correct. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects unusually clear scope, excellent direct responsiveness, and proportionate force, while leaving a narrow opening for a developed self-authenticating foundational account with independent explanatory resources.

sections.title: Secular Welfare and Impartial Rule Construction

pro.words: A secret assault upon an unconscious person remains wrong despite stipulated absence of awareness, pregnancy, disease, discovery, or immediate experiential harm.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The scenario pressures any narrowly experiential account by stipulating away awareness, pregnancy, disease, and discovery while preserving the strong judgment that violating an unconscious person remains gravely wrong. Principal limitation: The example construes harm too narrowly because autonomy, consent, rights, risk, potential interests, institutional rules, and social consequences can remain morally relevant even without later conscious awareness. Live burden: The challenge must engage the broader secular account actually presented and show that its potential-state or rule-level resources cannot explain the verdict, rather than defeating only immediate sensation maximization. Locked score: The supplied mixed band reflects a vivid and relevant counterexample with a stable central intuition, while its incomplete stipulations and restricted conception of harm prevent it from undermining welfare-sensitive secular theories generally.

con.words: Secular reasoning can assess actual and potential conscious states alongside rule-level social consequences, rather than maximizing only immediate aggregate happiness.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The response broadens secular evaluation beyond immediate aggregate sensation by explicitly incorporating actual and potential conscious states together with rule-level consequences, directly addressing the narrow target constructed by the hidden-assault example. Principal limitation: It offers a viable method rather than a completed foundation, leaving unresolved how competing states are weighted, why the method binds dissenters, and whether rights possess independent significance. Live burden: The account must formalize its aggregation and rule selection while explaining why potential interests and impartial consequences retain normative authority rather than merely practical usefulness. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects precise identification of overlooked evaluative dimensions, excellent responsiveness, and disciplined calibration, while acknowledging that methodological adequacy against the counterexample does not by itself prove categorical secular obligation.

pro.words: A crude recipient-preference theory assigns opposite moral statuses to similar conduct according to recipients' desires and therefore cannot provide an objective standard.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response identifies a defect in crude preference satisfaction: variable desires cannot establish moral status without considering consent, coercion, agency, welfare, and the act’s character. Principal limitation: It projects that criterion onto the broader secular account, incorporating impartiality, potential-consciousness analysis, and consequentialism, so the conclusion bypasses decisive elements of the immediate proposal. Live burden: The objection must confront the welfare-and-rule construction, showing how recipient variation defeats impartial criteria, rather than merely yielding different results when morally relevant conditions differ. Locked score: The supplied weak band reflects a relevant example, while expanded scope, diminished representation of the opposing position, and failure to engage the veil or rule-consequence mechanisms prevent it from establishing that secular objectivity is unavailable.

con.words: Perfectly rational contractors behind a veil of ignorance can construct impartial rules for social conduct without presupposing God's existence or authority.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The veil procedure supplies a concrete secular mechanism for impartial rule construction by depriving contractors of knowledge that would permit tailoring social principles to their own identities or advantages. Principal limitation: Hypothetical agreement among idealized rational choosers does not automatically bind actual agents, and the account leaves its assumptions about rationality, risk, admissible interests, and contractual authority insufficiently defended. Live burden: The proposal must explain why the modeled choice situation tracks moral reasons rather than strategic consensus and how its rules address vulnerable parties, disagreement, and nonparticipants. Locked score: The supplied very strong band recognizes a clear, relevant, and proportionately stated alternative to divine authority, while retaining important questions about idealization and the normative transition from impartial construction to genuine obligation.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and the Is-Ought Bridge

pro.words: Christian discourse contains prescriptions and an explicit ought, whereas an arbitrary atheistic system cannot derive binding prescriptions from descriptions alone.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response recognizes the exact is-ought issue and insists that a complete moral account requires genuinely prescriptive content rather than a collection of descriptions about consequences, preferences, or divine facts. Principal limitation: Possessing or stating a prescription is not equivalent to deriving or justifying it, and the phrases describing Christian success and atheistic arbitrariness conceal the normative premise that would perform the bridge. Live burden: The affirmative must articulate reasons connecting God's character, authority, or human ends to obligation and defend those reasons without presupposing the disputed ought. Locked score: The supplied weak band reflects direct engagement with a central burden and a recoverable intended contrast, while the missing entailment, unsupported categorical confidence, and incomplete representation of secular normative resources leave the claimed bridge unconstructed.

con.words: If God's goodness means only conformity to God's nature, that circular formulation supplies no independent rational reason for an agent to obey divine desires.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The argument translates a self-certification objection into practical rational obedience, demonstrating why saying that God conforms to God's nature may provide agents no justificatory reason for compliance. Principal limitation: Its concluding rejection extends beyond that narrower demonstration, because objective reasons might arise from goodness, authority, creation, gratitude, or flourishing, notwithstanding the formulation's omission. Live burden: The argument must distinguish justification from motivation and establish that the offered circular explanation fails, unless it confronts theistic accounts of normative authority. Locked score: The supplied very strong band recognizes the objection's direct extension, relevance, and argumentative clarity, while preserving the decisive qualification that one stated reason's failure does not eliminate every potentially available reason for obedience.

pro.words: People ought to act rightly because conformity to God's standard glorifies God, understood as the supreme and proper object of worship.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response advances beyond merely listing divine descriptions by offering an explicit proposed reason for conduct, namely that right action conforms to and glorifies the supreme object of worship. Principal limitation: The key claims remain self-certifying because calling God the right standard and proper object of worship does not independently explain why every agent ought to glorify or conform to God. Live burden: The affirmative must defend a normative premise connecting divine perfection, human nature, rightful authority, or flourishing to fitting worship and universal obligation. Locked score: The supplied mixed band recognizes meaningful contact with the demand for a reason and a clearly recoverable proposed bridge, while its underdefined concepts, categorical force, and circular dependence upon divine standardhood leave the authority of that reason insufficiently established.

con.words: Divine creation, power, moral-standard status, and punitive capacity are descriptions that do not by themselves entail that anyone ought to obey God.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply enumerates the exact divine facts offered and applies the is-ought distinction with disciplined scope, concluding only that creation, power, standardhood, and punishment do not by themselves entail obedience. Principal limitation: The criticism leaves open whether those facts combined with normative premises about rightful authority, perfect goodness, gratitude, flourishing, or humanity's proper end could support a duty. Live burden: The objection must continue demanding an explicit bridge while avoiding the stronger assertion that no Christian bridge can possibly be constructed from additional premises. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects exceptional precision, calibration, charity, and direct responsiveness to the affirmative's central normative-authority route, with its acknowledged opening for a developed argument functioning as appropriate scope rather than a defect in the targeted diagnosis.

pro.words: Because God knows every actual and potential fact, divine revelations may have relevant reasons that cognitively limited human agents cannot fully understand.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response properly emphasizes epistemic asymmetry and qualifies its conclusion, explaining why limited agents could reasonably expect an omniscient revealer to possess relevant considerations beyond their present understanding. Principal limitation: Superior information does not establish moral goodness, trustworthy purposes, or normative authority, so deference remains vulnerable to the same circular evaluation problem raised against the divine standard. Live burden: The argument must connect omniscience to reliability and rightful authority through defended premises rather than treating comprehensive factual knowledge as sufficient for morally binding revelation. Locked score: The supplied mixed band recognizes a coherent and appropriately qualified epistemic reply with substantial relevance, while reflecting its failure to establish that the knowledgeable communicator also constitutes the moral foundation or supplies obligations that agents should accept.

con.words: If consequences make actions right, omniscience makes God an informational intermediary who reports moral facts rather than the foundation producing their truth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply isolates a decisive category distinction between knowing every morally relevant consequence and constituting what makes an action right, directly following the affirmative's own appeal to end results. Principal limitation: Its conclusion is conditional upon the consequence-based explanation offered in that exchange and therefore does not independently defeat a separate divine-nature account in which God grounds the evaluative criterion. Live burden: The response must retain that conditional scope while clarifying whether secular consequence facts can themselves support normativity and how agents should weigh them. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects exceptionally sharp diagnosis, stable terminology, and comprehensive contact with the targeted inference, while recognizing that the informational-intermediary result addresses this specific omniscience argument rather than every possible account of divine moral grounding.

pro.words: God's knowledge of every outcome permits perfectly informed judgments and prescriptions about which actions agents should or should not perform.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The argument identifies omniscience's advantage for consequence evaluation, showing a divine source could apply an evaluative standard without the predictive limitations constraining human judgment. Principal limitation: Outcome knowledge supplies information rather than a value function, so factual prediction cannot determine which consequences are good, bad, permissible, obligatory, or decisive. Live burden: The affirmative must specify the evaluative criterion converting consequence knowledge into moral judgment, while distinguishing God's informational and advisory role from God's metaphysical truth-making role. Locked score: The supplied mixed band recognizes an account of application, but preserves the qualification that its evaluative premise remains unstated, making the move useful for moral knowledge and guidance yet incomplete support for the motion's necessary foundation.

pro.words: Torturing babies to death solely for personal pleasure is universally wrong, and God's revealed prohibition on murder supplies the standard supporting that judgment.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The example specifies conduct, motive, and universal scope with unusual clarity, establishing compelling common ground for discussing whether at least one moral judgment applies independently of individual approval. Principal limitation: Widespread agreement that the act is wrong does not discriminate among divine, realist, contractual, rights-based, or welfare foundations, and citing revelation mainly restates the affirmative explanation. Live burden: The argument must show why the verdict requires God's revelation or character rather than merely demonstrating that competing theories converge upon the same prohibition. Locked score: The supplied strong and competent band recognizes a forceful, precisely framed moral absolute and an explicit proposed standard, while preserving the decisive limitation that confidence in the verdict supplies comparatively little evidence for the uniqueness or necessity of the asserted foundation.

con.words: If a divine nature favored universal misery, defining morality by that nature would classify misery as moral independently of suffering, happiness, or health.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The conditional vividly tests whether nature-based morality is genuinely nonarbitrary by holding the theory's defining relation constant while varying the stipulated divine character toward universal misery. Principal limitation: The hypothetical depends upon the coherence of a misery-favoring being counting as God, and the exchange treats an apparent concession somewhat more conclusively than the modal premise warrants. Live burden: The objection must explain that necessary perfection cannot answer merely by definition unless goodness receives enough independent content to distinguish perfection from stipulated conformity. Locked score: The supplied very strong band reflects a precise, highly responsive challenge with appropriately conditional structure, while recognizing that its force remains partly dependent upon contested modal assumptions about divine identity, perfection, and possible natures.

pro.words: Inconsistency between Christian profession and practice does not undermine objective moral truth, because agents may knowingly violate requirements they acknowledge as valid.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply correctly distinguishes an agent's inconsistent practice from the truth of the moral proposition violated, blocking any inference from disobedience or hypocrisy to the nonexistence of objective morality. Principal limitation: The opponent's explicit test concerned whether belief supplies motivation, not whether noncompliance disproves moral ontology, so the diagnosis leaves the requested practical reason substantially unanswered. Live burden: The affirmative must preserve this valid truth-compliance distinction while separately explaining what reasons Christianity supplies and why those reasons bind or motivate the stipulated believer. Locked score: The supplied very strong band rewards a logically secure, precisely scoped distinction and strong diagnostic contact, while acknowledging that its success defeats only a possible ontological inference and does not complete the motivational or normative-authority response.

con.words: Even complete belief in Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself guarantee motivation to obey the divine prescriptions believed true.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The role-play grants the opponent's entire factual and moral framework while withholding compliance, thereby cleanly demonstrating that sincere belief in objective prescriptions does not logically guarantee corresponding motivation. Principal limitation: The discussion occasionally blends a justificatory reason, psychological motivation, and practical compulsion, although an agent may possess decisive objective reasons while remaining irrationally unmoved. Live burden: The objection must preserve its limited non-entailment conclusion and avoid treating motivational failure as evidence against moral truth or obligation themselves. Locked score: The supplied strong and competent band recognizes an effective counterexample, charitable premise preservation, and clear practical relevance, while reflecting the conceptual slippage among reason and motivation and the fact that the example does not refute objective duties or their possible justification.

strengths: Directly framed the motion around universal moral truth, nonarbitrariness, and the need for a foundation rather than limiting the exchange to vocabulary.
Presented a coherent divine-nature alternative to arbitrary command theory and connected omniscience to informed moral guidance.
Used the universal torture prohibition and the truth-compliance distinction effectively, producing the affirmative's clearest common-ground verdict and strongest diagnostic reply.
Recognized the is-ought burden and repeatedly attempted to connect divine revelation, character, and glory to prescription.

blunders.text: The necessity case often moved from challenges to selected secular proposals toward elimination of every nondivine foundation without establishing an exhaustive dichotomy.
The nature account repeatedly asserted God's standardhood without adequately answering why that nature is independently good, uniquely possible, or normatively authoritative.
Several replies conflated information, prescription, foundation, and obligation, leaving the central is-ought bridge incomplete.
The recipient-preference objection addressed a simplified view rather than the stronger potential-state and impartial-rule account already presented.

strengths: Separated arbitrary definition from objective application and preserved modest scope when describing welfare as a secular subject of inquiry.
Mounted precise modal and circularity challenges to the divine-nature account without claiming that a contrary divine nature was actual.
Developed positive secular resources through potential conscious states, rule consequences, and veil-of-ignorance construction.
Repeatedly distinguished moral foundation from information, belief, motivation, punishment, and compliance.
Isolated the missing normative premise in the divine-obedience argument with exceptional precision and directness.

blunders.text: The initial welfare definition did not itself establish why flourishing and reduced suffering possess universally binding authority.
The universal-misery hypothetical depended upon a contested possibility concerning divine identity and treated the opponent's apparent concession somewhat strongly.
The belief-without-motivation scenario occasionally blurred objective reasons, psychological motivation, and practical compulsion.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest divine-foundation case treats objective obligation as a relation between necessarily perfect practical reason, humanity's nature and ends, and God's rightful authority, rather than as mere conformity to an unexplained will.
premises: Some moral requirements purport to give every relevant agent reasons that do not disappear when personal desire, social approval, or immediate advantage changes.
A necessarily perfect God would possess complete knowledge, perfectly ordered practical reason, and no conflict between moral understanding, intention, and character.
If rational creatures are created with determinate capacities and ends, facts about their flourishing can provide objective reasons grounded in what those creatures are.
If God's prescriptions perfectly express those objective reasons, revelation communicates duties rather than making otherwise reasonless conduct obligatory by fiat.
Rightful creative authority can add role-relative obligations of trust, gratitude, and stewardship when its exercise consistently serves the objective good of created agents.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, if necessary divine perfection, creaturely ends, and rightful authority are defensible, God can unify moral truth, knowledge, and obligation without reducing goodness to arbitrary command.

newArguments.title: Constitutive Reasons and Creaturely Ends
newArguments.text: A divine account can answer the is-ought objection by distinguishing brute descriptions from facts that are constitutive of agency. If rational creatures necessarily depend upon truth, coherent deliberation, mutual recognition, and stable social trust to exercise their capacities, then they possess reasons to protect those goods. God need not manufacture those reasons through commands; divine creation establishes the kind of beings involved, while perfect practical wisdom recognizes and communicates what their flourishing requires. This makes revelation evidential and authoritative without treating sheer power as morality.

newArguments.title: Qualified Rightful Authority
newArguments.text: Creation alone does not entail obedience, but creation joined with perfect knowledge, unwavering concern for creaturely good, and legitimate governance may establish rightful authority. The relevant analogy is not ownership of an object; it is a fiduciary relationship in which authority is justified by competence, responsibility, and orientation toward the governed party's good. Divine prescriptions would then give agents additional role-relative reasons, while never converting harmful conduct into goodness merely because it was commanded. This directly answers the punishment-based caricature and places constraints upon what could count as divine authority.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest secular case treats morality as disciplined inquiry into reasons that mutually vulnerable agents can justify to one another under impartial conditions, without requiring a divine truth-maker.
premises: Conscious agents have empirically discoverable interests in avoiding severe suffering, preserving agency, maintaining trust, and accessing conditions necessary for meaningful choice.
A reason is not merely private when its supporting facts apply comparably to every similarly situated agent and survive correction for ignorance, coercion, and self-serving bias.
Rules chosen without knowledge of one's social identity provide a practical test of whether principles distribute risks and protections impartially.
Objective moral judgments can therefore concern whether conduct violates justified interests and impartial rules, even while the concepts used to describe morality remain conventional.
Adding divine commands or character does not improve this justification unless an independent bridge explains why divine conformity supplies reasons to affected agents.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, secular moral inquiry can support objective and revisable judgments through shared facts and impartial justification, while God's existence is not required for that limited achievement.

newArguments.title: Public Reasons Under Reciprocal Vulnerability
newArguments.text: Moral authority can arise from reciprocal justification among agents who are simultaneously capable of harming and being harmed. A proposed rule is deficient when it protects the speaker's interests while discounting equivalent interests of others without a relevant difference. This test is more than preference counting: evidence about pain, autonomy, dependency, deception, and institutional trust constrains which principles can be reciprocally defended. Because those facts remain true regardless of who occupies each social position, judgments based upon them can be objective in a practically important sense without requiring an external personal lawgiver.

newArguments.title: Independent Convergence as Evidence
newArguments.text: A secular account can treat convergence among distinct methods as evidence rather than making one chosen definition bear the entire foundational burden. Severe assault is condemned by welfare analysis because it predictably damages conscious interests, by contractualism because no exposed party could reasonably accept permission for it, by rights theory because it overrides bodily agency, and by rule analysis because tolerated violations destroy security and trust. Agreement across methods does not prove every verdict, but it reduces dependence on arbitrary stipulation and makes disagreement traceable to factual assumptions, weighting principles, or procedural defects that can be publicly examined.
